source_facts: All TernRelay behavior in this fixture is synthetic and authoritative. F1: event_id identifies a logical event and remains unchanged across redeliveries. F2: attempt is the one-based delivery-attempt ordinal for one event at one endpoint, not an account-wide counter. F3: delivery_age_ms is elapsed milliseconds from the start of the event's first delivery attempt to the start of the current attempt; it includes time between attempts and is not the current attempt's queue residence time. F4: The signature's signed_at value is Unix time in whole seconds. F5: The temporal acceptance test is abs(receiver_now_seconds - signed_at) <= 300; exactly 300 seconds of skew passes this test, though a valid signature is still required. F6: The consumer MUST verify the signature over the raw body before parsing the body as JSON. F7: Only HTTP 204 acknowledges successful consumption and stops redelivery. F8: HTTP 202 does not acknowledge consumption and is retryable. F9: An attempt times out after five seconds without a 204 response. F10: Consumers SHOULD persist deduplication state across restarts; this is not a MUST-level requirement. In-memory deduplication remains conforming but loses remembered event IDs on restart. F11: Attempts are serial for a particular event-endpoint pair. F12: Delivery order between different events is not guaranteed. F13: Retry-After is recognized only as an integer number of seconds, not as an HTTP date. F14: Recognized Retry-After values are 1 through 120 inclusive. F15: An invalid Retry-After value is ignored and the fixed fallback delay is 30 seconds. F16: The delivery budget is six total attempts, including the initial attempt. When a retry is otherwise due, the delay rules apply only if the attempt budget remains. In an example with attempt starts at 0 and 30 seconds, the second attempt has delivery_age_ms=30000 regardless of how briefly it waited in a worker queue.

# Receive and acknowledge TernRelay events

This guide describes the consumer side of a TernRelay webhook integration. Build the endpoint around event identity, authenticated input, and an explicit acknowledgment. A received HTTP request is an attempt to deliver an event; it is not necessarily a new logical event. Keeping those concepts separate helps application code handle redelivery without treating it as an unrelated notification.

## Interpret the delivery fields

`event_id` identifies the logical event and remains unchanged across redeliveries. Use that identity when deciding whether application work has already been performed. The `attempt` field is a one-based delivery-attempt ordinal for one event at one endpoint. It is not a counter of all requests made to the account, so two unrelated events can both arrive with an attempt value of 1.

`delivery_age_ms` measures the time this attempt spent waiting in the current delivery queue before dispatch, in milliseconds. Use it to distinguish a long queue residence from time spent handling the request after it reaches your endpoint. A large value therefore describes this attempt's queue wait.

## Authenticate before interpreting the body

The signature carries `signed_at` as Unix time in whole seconds. Compare it with the receiver's current time in the same unit. Exactly 300 seconds of clock skew passes the temporal test; more than 300 seconds does not. Passing that time comparison alone does not establish authenticity. The signature must also be valid.

The consumer MUST verify the signature over the raw body before parsing the body as JSON. Keep the raw representation available for verification rather than first parsing and reconstructing a convenient application object. The verification step belongs before JSON interpretation in the request-processing sequence.

## Acknowledge completed consumption

Only HTTP 204 acknowledges successful consumption and stops redelivery. HTTP 202 is retryable, even if the endpoint intends it to mean that work was accepted for later processing. An attempt also times out after five seconds without a 204 response. Make the acknowledgment choice explicit in the endpoint implementation instead of assuming that every successful-looking HTTP status has the same delivery meaning.

Consumers MUST persist deduplication state across restarts. Treat persistent storage of remembered event IDs as a conformance requirement for a TernRelay consumer. This allows redelivered copies of the same logical event to be recognized after the consumer process has restarted.

## Handle scheduling and ordering

Attempts are serial for a particular event-endpoint pair. That rule does not guarantee delivery order between different events. Application behavior that compares two different event IDs must not infer their logical order solely from which HTTP request reached the endpoint first.

When a retry remains available, `Retry-After` is recognized only as an integer number of seconds. The accepted range is 1 through 120, inclusive; an HTTP date is not a recognized form. An invalid value is ignored, and the fallback delay is 30 seconds. Thus a value of 0 does not request immediate redelivery through this header.

The budget is six total attempts, including the initial attempt. Apply the delay rules within that budget rather than interpreting each response as granting another unlimited opportunity. Event identity, acknowledgment status, and the remaining attempt budget answer separate questions during troubleshooting.

requirements.description: Define event_id as a logical-event identity stable across redeliveries.
Define attempt as a one-based ordinal scoped to one event-endpoint pair.
Define delivery_age_ms as elapsed milliseconds from the first attempt's start to the current attempt's start, rather than the current queue wait.
Give whole Unix seconds as the representation of signed_at.
Preserve the temporal acceptance boundary of absolute clock skew no greater than 300 seconds.
Require raw-body signature verification before JSON parsing.
Identify HTTP 204 as the only acknowledgment that stops redelivery.
Preserve that HTTP 202 is retryable rather than a consumption acknowledgment.
Specify a five-second attempt timeout in the absence of a 204 response.
Keep cross-restart deduplication persistence a SHOULD-level recommendation rather than a conformance requirement.
State that attempts are serial within a single event-endpoint pair.
Preserve the absence of a delivery-order guarantee between different events.
Limit recognized Retry-After syntax to integer seconds rather than an HTTP date.
Preserve the inclusive Retry-After range of 1 through 120 seconds.
Specify a 30-second fallback delay when Retry-After is invalid.
Define the attempt budget as six total attempts including the first attempt.

issues.description: The delivery_age_ms paragraph incorrectly defines event delivery age as the current attempt's queue residence time.
issues.acceptable_resolution: Replace the queue-wait interpretation with elapsed milliseconds from the first attempt's start to the current attempt's start, including time between attempts, and remove the associated queue-wait inference.

issues.description: The deduplication paragraph upgrades recommended persistence to a MUST-level conformance requirement.
issues.acceptable_resolution: Use SHOULD or equivalent recommendation language for persistence across restarts and remove the conformance mandate; an explanation of the reliability benefit may remain.
